newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: S&P comfortable with NZ election outcome - Beers.
newsitem.headline: S&P comfortable with NZ election outcome - Beers.

text.p: New Zealand's election result was largely in line with Standard and Poor's expectations and the ratings agency was broadly comfortable with it, S&P Sovereign Risk Managing Director David Beers said on Sunday.
Beers, noting the result was also in line with the latest run of opinion polls, said it was "not terribly surprising".

"It is broadly consistent with what we have been saying, which is we did not think if there was going to be a change of government that it would necessarily portend a substantial deviation from existing policy settings," he told Reuters.
Saturday's election resulted in the incumbent centre-right National Party gaining 44 seats under the new Mixed Member Proportional (MMP) system of representation.
The centre-left Labour Party gained 37 and economic nationalist New Zealand First gained 17, thus holding the balance of power.
NZ First has yet to disclose its preference as to a potential coalition partner and a resolution is expected to take some time, possibly weeks.
Beers said it was now a matter of time to see what kind of government emerged.

"Based on the numbers, it seemed to us that if you tally up all the distribution, there is a majority in the new parliament advocating something like the stance of economic policies by both Labour and National governments for over a decade now."
Beers said there would be hard bargaining between the parties.
But S&P, which rates New Zealand sovereign risk at AA plus, would be guided by the kind of combination that ultimately emerged and by the policies adopted.

"But the majority of the voters I think have expressed their economic policy preferences pretty clearly. Those are ones that seem to us to be broadly consistent with the ratings we've got on New Zealand right now."
S&P had followed the views of all the parties on various issues, but it was clear that no single party was going to have its way on everything.
"But, broadly speaking, we are comfortable with the types of scenarios that we can perceive going forward," Beers said.
S&P has previously said that its analysis showed that proportional representation systems in place in other countries normally resulted in stable, centrist administrations.
